But the real question is how they learned from the philosophers.
Did they simply take philosophical ideas from outside and copy them mechanically?
Or did philosophy enter into an active process of interaction and internal development within Arab-Islamic thought itself?
It seems clear to us that the second is what happened.
The Muʿtazilites began from the intellectual foundation we have just described, built on two principles of their own.
The first was divine unity, which came from religious and metaphysical thought.
The second was the insistence that reason should be the primary judge when divine unity was being understood.
This second principle grew out of the Muʿtazilites’ own position within the intellectual and cultural development of their society during a highly dynamic historical period.
It also grew out of the social and political conditions from which their Qadarite and Jabrite predecessors had emerged.
When Muʿtazilite ideas and knowledge later came into contact with the philosophers and with ancient philosophical sources, the Muʿtazilites did not take their basic starting point from those sources.
What they took, first, was method.
Second, they took the new intellectual tools that philosophical learning placed at their disposal.
These tools gave them a new ability to use rational arguments and logical methods in support of principles that had already arisen from their own specifically Islamic position.
They had inherited that position from earlier Muslim thinkers.
Those earlier thinkers had gradually built up a new body of ideas, one step at a time.
The first raw material for this development came mainly from the great political crisis created by the struggle over the caliphate.
That political conflict was deeply and organically connected with religious thought and with practical religious positions as well.

The claim that Muʿtazilite ideas about God’s attributes and the created Qurʾān came from Jewish, Christian or Persian Manichaean thought is another question, and one that deserves some discussion within the limits of the sources now available to us.

It has been said, for example, that belief in the created Qurʾān probably came from the Jewish belief that the Torah was created, while belief in an eternal Qurʾān resembles the Christian doctrine of the eternal Word.
But where does this claim come from?
We have already seen that Jahm ibn Ṣafwān believed that the Qurʾān was created.
The question therefore did not begin with the Muʿtazilites.
It is also known that al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham held this view before Jahm, and that Jahm was influenced by him.
Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn Kathīr and others report this.

These sources say that al-Jaʿd took the idea of the created Qurʾān from Bayān ibn Samʿān, who took it from Ṭālūt, the nephew of Labīd. Labīd, in turn, was the nephew of al-Aʿṣam, who had been an opponent of the Prophet and had lived during the rise of Islam.
The whole point of producing this chain seems to be to reach Ibn Kathīr’s final conclusion: that Labīd himself took the doctrine of the created Qurʾān from a Jew in Yemen.
And so Jahm took it from al-Jaʿd, al-Jaʿd from Bayān, Bayān from Ṭālūt, Ṭālūt was Labīd’s nephew, Labīd was al-Aʿṣam’s nephew, and al-Aʿṣam was an enemy of the Prophet.

We are therefore expected to search for a source that is both non-Islamic and hostile to Islam until, at the end of the chain, we finally discover a Jew in Yemen who supposedly introduced this heresy into Islam!
Scientific historical research cannot accept an artificial chain like this without solid historical evidence.
There is also evidence that directly weakens the supposed connection between the created Qurʾān and Judaism.
The doctrine arose among its supporters from an intense desire to preserve the absolute purity of divine unity and to deny every form of bodily existence to God.
Judaism, by contrast, contains the idea that when God spoke to Moses, He appeared to him in some form and Moses saw Him physically.
That stands in complete opposition to the theory of those who defended the created Qurʾān, from al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham to the most important early and later Muʿtazilite thinkers.
Early historians even report that al-Jaʿd himself was killed by the Umayyad governor of Kūfa, Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī, on the charge that he said:
“God did not truly speak to Moses.”
There is another claim found uniquely in Ibn al-Nadīm’s al-Fihrist.
He says that al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham was the tutor of Marwān ibn Muḥammad, the last Umayyad caliph in the eastern Islamic world, and that al-Jaʿd “led him into zandaqa.”
In that period, the word zandaqa most often referred to Manichaeism, which was widespread in Persia.
There is no historical evidence to support this claim.
There is no meaningful similarity between the doctrine that the Qurʾān is created—a doctrine based on divine unity—and Manichaeism, which rests on the idea of two divine principles.
A third claim remains. This is especially common among later researchers, though it ultimately goes back to earlier writers such as Ibn Taymiyya.
According to this view, al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham, from whom Jahm ibn Ṣafwān took the doctrine of the created Qurʾān, was influenced by the Sabians or by Christianity.
This influence may have been direct, or it may have come indirectly through Christian churches that had themselves absorbed ideas from the Greek Stoics.
We therefore have not one claim but three:
al-Jaʿd was influenced by the Sabians;
or by Stoicism through the Daysanite and Christian churches.
How well do these claims agree with the historical and theoretical evidence?
In theory, some Sabian influence is possible.
By “Sabians” here we mean the Harranians: the scholars—or more accurately, the priests—of the school of Ḥarrān in al-Jazīra, in northern Syria.
They later played a well-known role in transmitting Greek science into Arabic during the great translation movement.
We know that when the Arab conquest took place, the school of Ḥarrān already had links with ancient Greek mathematics and astronomy and had been influenced by Pythagorean and Neoplatonic theories.
For this reason, it was later able to contribute to the Arabic translation movement during the scientific flowering of the early ʿAbbāsid period.
The Harranians also seem to have formed a distinct religious community, and divine unity was one of the basic principles of their doctrine.

Ibn al-Nadīm tells us that in the age of al-Kindī, the “philosopher of the Arabs,” they possessed a book containing their teachings on divine unity. They attributed this book to Hermes, whom they regarded as one of their prophets.
Ibn al-Nadīm reports that al-Kindī described it as:
“a work of the highest perfection in its treatment of divine unity, whose teachings a philosopher, however hard he tries, can hardly avoid accepting.”
Al-Bīrūnī also writes of the Harranians:

“What we know of these people is only that they affirm the oneness of God and declare Him free from imperfections. They apply the beautiful names to Him metaphorically, because in their view He has no attributes in the literal sense. They assign the ordering of the world to the celestial sphere and its bodies, and they say that these are alive, speaking, hearing and seeing. They also venerate light.”
From these two sources, al-Kindī and al-Bīrūnī, we can see that the Harranians affirmed divine unity.
So in theory, it is possible that someone like al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham could have been influenced by them.
The evidence makes it difficult to believe that al-Jaʿd could have known the details of Harranian doctrine at such an early date.
Al-Jaʿd was killed in the third decade of the second Islamic century, around the middle of the eighth century CE.
Yet Ibn al-Nadīm’s own account tells us that the Harranian book containing their teachings on divine unity appeared in the time of al-Kindī.
And al-Kindī lived from the end of the second Islamic century until after the middle of the third, roughly from the early ninth century until late in that century.

This suggests that Arab thinkers became familiar with the basic features of Harranian doctrine only after the question of the created Qurʾān had already appeared with al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham and then Jahm ibn Ṣafwān.
Christianity is equally difficult to accept as the original source of the problem.

The general Muʿtazilite approach to God’s attributes, and especially to the created Qurʾān, was clearly aimed not only at protecting God from multiplicity but also at denying every possible form of embodiment or indwelling.

Yet the Christian doctrines that could have influenced Arab and Muslim intellectual centres at the time were known to Muslim thinkers above all through the Trinity and through the idea that God dwelt in Christ and appeared through him.
Moreover, to say that the Qurʾān was created is to deny the eternity of the Word of God.
Christian doctrine, by contrast, affirms the eternity of the Word.
The two positions are therefore opposed.
If Christian influence must be admitted—and there is nothing strange about cultural influence of this kind—then the more likely form is negative influence.
In other words, the theory of the created Qurʾān may have developed partly as a response to the Christian doctrine of the eternal Word, rather than as an imitation of it.
This seems the more likely possibility.
For the same reason that we ruled out Manichaeism as the source of the doctrine, we also rule out the Daysanites.
Manichaeism and the Daysanite doctrine rest on the same basic principle: dualism.
Mani ibn Fātik al-Ḥakīm, from whom Manichaeism takes its name, held that:
“The world is made from two eternal principles: one light and the other darkness.”
“affirmed two principles, light and darkness. Light produces good intentionally and by choice, while darkness produces evil naturally and by necessity.”
The conflict with the Muʿtazilite principle of divine unity is obvious.
We should emphasize once again what we are—and are not—arguing here.
When we criticize claims that the questions of God’s attributes and the created Qurʾān came from outside sources, we are not denying outside influence in general.
We are denying it only as the original source for those Muslim thinkers who raised these questions before the Muʿtazilites.
Second, our argument does not mean that we believe cultures develop in isolation from one another.
